name: PT Archi Indonesia Tbk

frontmatter.title: Archi Indonesia: the plant, not the orebody, is the binding constraint
frontmatter.summary: Archi runs the Toka Tindung gold mine in North Sulawesi under two Contracts of Work. The orebody has been there for years; the mill has not. A three-phase expansion takes throughput from four to six million tonnes a year, and every extra ounce drops through a cost base that has already fallen sharply. The shares discount a mine that never grows. We initiate at ADD.
thesis: Throughput, not geology, sets the earnings path: the three-phase plant expansion lifts capacity by half again while the reserve grade leaves room for higher recovered ounces.
The cost base has already reset: cash cost per ounce fell from the FY2025 average to the first-half level as volumes rose, so incremental ounces carry a much wider margin than the trailing print.
The depleting-asset discount is too wide: a life-of-reserve valuation on the reviewed metals deck leaves a double-digit return even though the market already assumes a through-cycle gold price.
The risks are real and named: a fixed-life Contract of Work, a higher statutory royalty, a controlling shareholder with a thin free float and a related-party mining contractor.

catalysts.event: Quarterly operating update: ore processed, grade and the first plant phase run-rate
Full-year results and the declaration of the next cash dividend
Second-phase expansion commissioning and Kopra underground development progress
Reserve and resource restatement converting part of the measured resource into reserve

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of Archi Indonesia at ADD with a twelve-month target of Rp1,179, 13.4% above the Rp1,040 last price and a total expected return of 17.1% once the 39 rupiah a share of dividends we expect over the year is included [S2][S3]. The call is not a gold-price call: our valuation uses the reviewed metals deck, whose through-cycle mark sits above the spot price. Read back on the base model, the share price implies a benchmark a little below that mark — the market is already pricing a mine that never grows, not a higher gold price [S0]. The upside comes from volume and unit cost, the two things the company controls.

The asset is the Toka Tindung gold mine in North Sulawesi, held through two Contracts of Work that together cover 39,817 hectares [S7][S2]. Management is taking processing capacity from four million tonnes a year to six in three phases across FY2026 to FY2028, with the Kopra underground mine developed alongside [S5]. Six million tonnes a year, at the 1.0 grams per tonne head grade the mine actually ran in the first half of FY2026 and the 89 percent recovery the company reports, supports roughly 170 thousand ounces of annual output, against 124 thousand ounces sold in FY2025 [S5][S8][S2]. That is the base case and it is deliberately below the orebody: feed at the one point two grams per tonne reserve grade would add roughly a sixth to recovered ounces, which we carry as bull-case upside rather than in the base [S8][S5].

What the market pays for that is a depleting asset with a fixed licence horizon. At the last price the equity is worth IDR26,244.4bn and the enterprise value is 5.1x our FY2026E EBITDA of US$365.1m [S0]. That is a discount to what a long-life, high-margin gold mine would normally command, and it is the discount we think is too wide once the plant is running.

Three things move the value. First, ore throughput and grade: the model's value is roughly linear in ounces sold, and the base case already assumes a grade below the reserve grade, so there is room for upside without assuming new ounces [S8]. Second, the cash cost per ounce, which has fallen as volumes rose and which is the difference between a wide margin and a thin one at any gold price [S3]. Third, the discount rate and the licence: a Contract of Work to 2041 with two ten-year extensions available is not a perpetual asset, and we value it as a life-of-reserve stream with no terminal value [S2].

Indonesian gold mining sits at the meeting point of two regimes: a mining law that grants mineral rights by contract or by licence, and a fiscal regime that taxes the metal through a royalty tied to the international reference price. The sector has consolidated around a handful of producing assets, each with its own tenure, grade and cost position, and each priced by the market largely on remaining life and cash cost rather than on headline production. Gold itself is priced globally in dollars, so a domestic producer's rupiah revenue moves with the exchange rate as well as with the metal, while part of the cost base is domestic. That asymmetry is why gold miners in emerging markets trade at a discount to their developed-market peers.

Archi Indonesia is a gold producer. Its operating asset is the Toka Tindung mine in the Minahasa region of North Sulawesi, worked through two Contracts of Work held by PT Meares Soputan Mining and PT Tambang Tondano Nusajaya, covering 39,817 hectares in total [S7][S2]. The group reports three segments: gold mining, which supplied US$435.8m of external revenue in FY2025; a precious-metals trading and refining business operated through PT Emas Mineral Murni; and a small residual segment that loses money [S2]. Gold is overwhelmingly the business, and the trading arm exists largely to place the mine's output and to sell refined metal on.

The mining operation is conventional open pit with an expanding underground component. In the first half of FY2026 the company mined 20 million tonnes of total material, processed 2.0 million tonnes of ore at a head grade of 1.0 grams per tonne and a recovery of 89 percent, and produced 60 thousand ounces of gold [S5]. That is a high-strip, high-volume operation: the ratio of material mined to ore processed is roughly ten to one, which is why the mining-services contract and diesel are two of the largest items in the cost base [S5][S2]. Grade at the reserve is about one point two grams per tonne, and the process plant is a standard crush-grind-leach circuit with the recovery the company reports [S8][S5].

The strategy is a capacity story. The company is expanding the plant from four million tonnes a year to six in three phases, with the first phase in FY2026, the second in FY2027 and the third commissioning in FY2028 [S5]. Alongside it, the Kopra underground mine is being developed at a grade of roughly six grams per tonne, and the open pit continues to supply the bulk of the feed [S5]. Management guides FY2026 gold production fifteen to twenty percent above the FY2025 outturn [S4]. The company is also developing a geothermal project through PT Toka Tindung Geothermal, a strategic national project with a target capacity of forty megawatts that would supply both the mine and the grid, which matters more for cost and emissions than for value in the near term [S6].

The customer base is narrow and the buyer is domestic. The five largest customers took 75 percent of FY2025 revenue, and the largest single customer took 30.9 of it [S2]. That is normal for an Indonesian gold miner selling doré and refined metal into a small pool of licensed buyers, but it means pricing is set by reference to the international market rather than negotiated, and it means the loss of one buyer is a receivable and logistics problem rather than a demand problem.

A gold miner's economics are simple in structure and brutal in detail: revenue is ounces sold times the dollar price, and cost is tonnes moved, tonnes processed and grade. The plant is the fixed constraint. When a mill runs below capacity the mine carries its fixed cost over fewer ounces, and when it runs at capacity the same fixed cost is spread further. That is why expansions in this industry are so valuable at the margin, and why the market watches throughput data more closely than it watches production guidance. Grade is the other lever, and it is the one the geology controls rather than management.

The product is a globally priced commodity and the company is a price taker. The reviewed metals deck carries gold at 4,300 dollars an ounce for the through-cycle year, against a current-year mark of 4,494 and a FY2025 average realised price of 3,528 dollars an ounce on the company's own sales [S0][S6]. That marker is the sourced through-cycle input the method requires — the house's reviewed series, not a broker forecast — and it sits above both the spot price and the FY2025 realised average. We are therefore valuing the mine at a cycle position above spot, not below it, and the risk section shows what a lower gold price does to the value [S0]. The deck also carries silver, which matters marginally because the orebody produces a silver by-product [S0]. Nothing about Archi's position changes the gold price, so the industry question is really a cost-curve and tenure question.

On cost, the only independent ranking the company publishes is dated and favourable: the prospectus reports CRU placing Toka Tindung at the bottom of the first quartile of the global all-in sustaining cost curve in 2019 [S8]. The FY2025 all-in sustaining cost of US$1,841/oz is well above the level that earned that place, and no current quartile is disclosed, so we treat the position as unproven rather than repeat the older claim [S6][S8]. Our own build from the segment note, which strips out the trading business and the royalty, puts cash cost at a little over a thousand dollars an ounce in FY2025 and below that in the first half of FY2026 as volumes rose [S2][S3]. At the deck's through-cycle gold price that is a very wide margin, and it is the margin that funds the expansion.

The regulatory regime has tightened in a way that is specific and quantifiable. PP 19/2025 raised the gold royalty to 16% of the reference price once the international benchmark reaches three thousand dollars an ounce, up from ten percent under the earlier regulation [S9]. The audited accounts confirm the higher rates applied from April 2025, and the first half of FY2026 royalty line is consistent with the rate now in force [S4][S3]. This is a real, permanent transfer from the mine to the state, and we model it as flat rather than assuming any relief.

Tenure is the other industry fact that matters. The Contracts of Work run to 2041 and may be extended twice by ten years in the form of an IUPK, which the company states in its own filings [S2]. A licence that ended in 2041 without extension would cut the reserve life short, so the extension is not a formality to be assumed lightly; we model the reserve, not the licence, as the binding constraint, and the reserve runs out inside the extended window rather than at the end of the current contract [S8].

The competitive landscape is thin. The listed domestic peer set in precious and base metals is effectively one name, which is why we weight valuation entirely to a life-of-reserve DCF rather than to a peer median [S0]. Archi's differentiation is grade and scale against cost: it is one of a small number of Indonesian gold mines producing at this volume, with a reserve grade above the global average for open-pit gold and a cost position that is competitive internationally [S8][S6]. Its weakness is life and ownership: a single asset, a single jurisdiction, a controlling shareholder and a finite contract.

Gold miners are valued on remaining life, cost position and jurisdiction, in roughly that order. A mine with a long reserve and a low cost trades at a premium to one with the same current earnings and a shorter life, because the market is buying a stream of ounces rather than a year of profit. Jurisdiction enters as a discount rate rather than as a line item: contract tenure, royalty regime, permitting and the risk of renegotiation all show up as a higher cost of capital. That is why two mines with identical cost curves can trade at very different multiples, and why the market pays so much attention to reserve replacement.

The reported history is a story about price, not volume. Gold sold was 117 thousand ounces in FY2022, 121 in FY2023, 97 in FY2024 and 124 in FY2025, while the average selling price went from 1,810 to 1,951 to 2,401 to 3,528 dollars an ounce over the same years [S6]. Revenue followed the price: the group turned over US$287.6m in FY2024 and US$496.2m in FY2025, with EBITDA of US$74.6m and US$226.7m respectively [S2]. The FY2024 dip in ounces, when the mine sold 97 thousand ounces against a reserve that supports far more, is the clearest evidence that the plant has been the constraint.

The first thing to fix in the data is depreciation. The data pack carries only a fragment of the operating-expense depreciation line for FY2025, orders of magnitude below the real charge; the segment note in the audited accounts shows total D&A of US$25.3m, against US$21.2m in FY2024 [S2]. We restate both years and carry D&A forward at the segment rate per ounce [S2]. This matters for the earnings bridge and for the tax charge, not for cash flow, because free cash flow is built from EBIT plus D&A less capex and the split between the two is neutral.

The second thing to fix is the cost base. Consolidated cost of goods sold includes the trading arm's cost of purchased metal, which has nothing to do with the cost of an ounce of gold; building a unit cost off consolidated COGS overstates mine cost by roughly half. We rebuild it from the segment note instead: gold segment revenue less segment operating profit less segment D&A less the royalty line gives a cash cost of a little over a thousand dollars an ounce in FY2025, falling below a thousand in the first half of FY2026 as throughput rose [S2][S3]. The company's own all-in sustaining cost series, which adds royalty and sustaining capex to that base, corroborates the arithmetic [S6]. We carry a flat nominal unit cost to FY2030E and let the engine escalate it thereafter, which is deliberately not a forecast of further efficiency gains. The cost step is disclosed rather than buried: the FY2026E re-price carries EBITDA of US$365.1m against the FY2025 actual of US$226.7m, and the difference comes from resetting the unit cost to the first-half level on higher throughput, not from price or volume [S3][S2]. The base volume of 170 thousand ounces is six million tonnes at about the first half's head grade, not at the reserve grade; at the reserve grade the same plant would support materially more ounces, which is an upside case and not the base [S5][S8].

The forecast is a volume ramp on a fixed price path. For FY2026 we take the 55 thousand ounces actually sold in the first half and add a second half at the run-rate implied by management's production guidance, for 132 thousand ounces [S5][S4]. The plant then steps to 150 and 165 thousand ounces as the phases commission, and settles at 170 thousand ounces, which is the six-million-tonne rate at a grade deliberately below the reserve grade [S5][S8]. Revenue reaches US$748.8m in FY2026E and US$909.1m by FY2029E, with EBITDA of US$365.1m and US$445.4m [S5].

Cash flow and the balance sheet are the part the market underrates. Capex is front-loaded: US$114.0m in FY2026E against D&A of US$29.0m, split between sustaining spend and the expansion programme, and falling to US$47.4m by FY2030E once the build is done [S5][S3]. Net debt was US$469.8m at the FY2025 year end and US$424.4m at the end of FY2026E, falling every year as the corporate facility amortises, and the model has the group in net cash from FY2030E [S3][S2]. We model 1.2x of net debt to EBITDA at the end of FY2026E against 2.1x a year earlier, which is comfortable for an asset with this margin.

Capital allocation is a rising dividend on a falling debt balance. The company paid US$30.0m of dividends in FY2025, about thirty percent of attributable profit, and has since paid two cash dividends [S4][S0]. We hold the payout at that observed rate rather than assuming either a special distribution or a step-up, which leaves cash accumulating in the later years of the model. That cash is not lost to the valuation: an enterprise-value DCF counts every year's free cash flow, so the flat payout is a distribution-policy assumption, not a hidden discount [S2]. The capacity anchor the method asks for is the free-cash-flow yield of 2.0% against a dividend yield of 3.7% at the modelled payout, which is what the market would pay for the stream if it believed the ramp [S0][S2].

The earnings-quality flags are identifiable rather than alarming. Related-party purchases from a mining-services associate were US$61.6m in FY2025, about a fifth of cost of goods sold, so a material share of the cost base is transacted with a party the group partly owns [S2]. Customer concentration is high, with the top five buyers at 75 percent of revenue [S2]. Accruals do not show a persistent divergence between profit and operating cash flow once the working-capital swings are allowed for, and the FY2025 accounts carry an unmodified opinion [S2]. The thing to watch is the gold-price sensitivity of working capital: inventory and payables move with the metal, which makes a single-year working-capital ratio a poor guide and is why we carry the last audited ratio rather than the three-year average [S2].

A depleting mine should be valued as a finite stream of cash flows, so the primary method is a life-of-reserve DCF with an explicit horizon to FY2046E and no terminal value [S8]. The reserve is the weakest link in the published record, and we restate it. The only reserve statement the company has registered is the SRK estimate reprinted in the 2021 IPO prospectus, dated 31 December 2020 [S8]. It reports 3,900 thousand ounces then; production since has depleted it and no newer table has been published. The arithmetic: 2,520 thousand ounces produced cumulatively between 2011 and 2025 [S4] less the 2,100 thousand ounces the prospectus already counted as depleted to the end of 2020 [S8] gives the production the 2021 estimate does not reflect, leaving 3,480 thousand ounces at the start of FY2026 [S8][S4]. We assume no reserve additions from the 2025 drilling campaign or the Kopra underground, so conversion is upside rather than base [S4][S7]. The reserve depletes in FY2046E and the DCF stops there. That horizon runs past the 2041 Contract of Work expiry, so the plan already carries the first ten-year extension; the reserve, not the licence, binds [S2].

The cost of capital is built from the reviewed macro deck rather than from a company-specific guess. The risk-free rate is 4.9%, the mature-market equity premium 4.2% and the Indonesia country premium 2.5%, with an unlevered beta of 1.0 that levers to 1.26 at the group's market debt to equity of 0.34 [S0]. That gives a cost of equity of 13.6% and a weighted average cost of capital of 11.5%, which is inside the house bounds [S0]. The engine prices the debt off a generic corporate spread at 6.9%, below the rate the company actually pays on its drawn facility, so we add a small company financing premium to the cost of equity to keep the discount rate honest [S2][S3].

The DCF produces a fundamental value of Rp1,149 a share and an enterprise value of US$2,069.2m, with no terminal value contributing [S8]. The bridge from enterprise value to equity is simple: net debt at the last balance sheet, with no minority or associate deduction large enough to matter [S3]. On a per-ounce basis the enterprise value of US$2,069.2m against 3,480 thousand reserve ounces is a small fraction of the deck's gold price per ounce; we show the two inputs rather than a ratio because the engine carries no EV-per-reserve line, and the gap to the gold price is the market's discount for a single asset, a finite contract and a reserve the company has not restated [S8][S0]. At the spot gold price rather than the deck marker the same model is worth less — the sensitivity grid's lower price steps are that value — so our target is a through-cycle NAV, not a spot-price mark [S0].

The cross-checks are shown and rejected rather than quietly dropped. The peer set in this industry is effectively one listed name, which is below the house's threshold for a median, and book value is not a value anchor for an asset whose equity is small against its gross property and whose reserves are consumed every year [S0][S2]. We therefore weight the DCF at one hundred percent and disclose the change from the industry default, rather than blending in a multiple we do not believe [S2].

Sensitivity is dominated by the gold price, as it must be for a producer with a wide margin. A twenty percent move in the benchmark moves the value by well over forty percent — the grid is close to two-to-one in gold, reflecting a fixed cost base and a flat royalty — and volume moves it in the same direction with a smaller elasticity [S0]. The grid is re-run with a flat shocked driver path, so its centre sits materially below the base-case value of Rp1,149: it is a relative map, not a set of alternative targets, and the level difference is about a sixth, not a rounding [S0].

The reverse DCF says something useful about what is already in the price, once its convention is stated. The engine solves the implied benchmark on that same flat price path, not on the base path, so the solved 4,427 dollars an ounce overstates the base-model equivalent [S0]. Re-solved on the base model — value Rp1,149 at the deck against a Rp1,040 share price — the market implies a benchmark slightly below the deck marker rather than at or above it. The share price is therefore discounting the mine, not marking gold up, and it is not paying for the expansion either. That is the right frame for the call, and it is why the thesis rests on throughput and unit cost rather than on the metal.

The largest risk is the gold price, and it is unavoidable. The reserve is finite, part of the cost base is fixed in dollars, and a twenty percent lower benchmark cuts our value by well over forty percent [S0]. Our base price is the deck's marker, which sits above spot and above the FY2025 realised average, so the risk is cycle position rather than a discount we have already taken: the bear at a fifth below the deck is a near-cycle case, not a full mean reversion to the long-run realised gold price, and at such a level the value would fall below the bear target [S0]. We do not hedge that risk in the model, and we do not assume a price above the reviewed deck to manufacture upside.

The second risk is tenure, and we value the cut rather than describe it. The Contract of Work runs to 2041 and the extensions are discretionary acts of the state, not contractual rights, even where the company describes them as available [S2]. The restated reserve of 3,480 thousand ounces does not deplete at the licence boundary: at the 170 thousand-ounce run-rate it lasts to FY2046E, so five modelled years — FY2042E to FY2046E, at the same annual rate — sit beyond the current term, and the plan already carries the first ten-year extension [S2][S8]. Closing the mine at the 2041 expiry in the same model, with everything else held, lowers the enterprise value from US$2,069.2m by about an eighth and the value per share from Rp1,149 by roughly a sixth, because the valuation has no terminal value and those five years are pure free cash flow [S0]. The twelve-month target would sit about a sixth below the base target of Rp1,267 and far above the bear of Rp463: material enough to monitor, not enough to carry alone. The company cites no condition or probability for the extensions beyond the right to request them twice, and we assume only the first because the reserve is exhausted before the second could be used [S2][S8]. Related to it is the royalty: PP 19/2025 lifted the gold take to 16% at high prices, and a further increase is a policy choice rather than a commercial one [S9][S4].

The third risk is operational. The ramp depends on the plant phases commissioning on schedule and on the Kopra underground reaching its grade [S5]. A slippage of a year is worth roughly a tenth of the value, and a grade shortfall at Kopra compounds it because the underground was meant to lift the blended grade. Cost inflation in mining services, diesel and labour is a real risk for a high-strip operation, although the recent trend in unit cost has been down [S3][S6].

The fourth risk is governance and liquidity. The controlling shareholder holds 71.9% of the company and the free float is 15.8% of the shares, with related-party purchases equal to about a fifth of cost of goods sold [S4][S0][S2]. Related-party terms are disclosed and audited, but the minority's protection rests on process rather than on a blocking stake, and a thin float amplifies any move in the share price in both directions. Traded value averages IDR47.6bn a day against a 15.8% float, which is comfortable for the fund's liquidity rules at current volumes, so we apply no liquidity discount; the float is thin enough that the discount would matter if the daily value halved, and that is the trigger to revisit [S0].

We weight the scenarios at 25% bear, 50% base and 25% bull. The bear value of Rp463 assumes gold twenty percent below the deck's through-cycle mark and volume ten percent under base as the expansion slips; the bull value of Rp1,720 assumes gold twenty percent above it and volume ten percent higher as Kopra lifts the blend and the plant runs above the base grade [S0][S8]. The shocks are mirrored and the probabilities symmetric, which is the house rule, and the asymmetry in the values comes from operating leverage rather than from a different set of assumptions in each case.

Control is concentrated and disclosed. PT Rajawali Corpora holds 71.9% of the shares and a second Rajawali vehicle holds a further block, leaving a public float of 15.8% [S4][S0]. The group is part of the Rajawali conglomerate, but it is not a konglo overlay name under the house registry, so no konglo discount is applied to the target [S0]. The board and management are the controlling shareholder's appointees, which is normal for an Indonesian family-controlled producer and is the reason the related-party note matters more here than in a widely held company.

The listing and structure flags are checkable. The shares are on the exchange's main trading board rather than the special monitoring board [S4], and in the filings we reviewed we found no notation letter or special monitoring status. We also found no reported pledge over the Rajawali block: the annual report sets out the pledged-share reporting regime without disclosing a pledge on the controlling stake, and we report that as an absence of disclosure rather than as a clean bill [S4]. The corporate action in train is a refinancing, not an equity raise: the first-half accounts were prepared for a planned public offering of debt securities, so the contingency is a debt rollover rather than dilution [S3].

Related-party dealings are material and quantified. The group buys mining services from PT Geopersada Mulia Abadi, an associate held through a joint venture, for US$61.6m in FY2025, and the associate pays a dividend back to the group [S2]. The transactions are disclosed with the comparison percentages an auditor would want, and the FY2025 opinion is unmodified [S2]. Dividends have been paid regularly, including an interim distribution of US$30.0m in FY2025 and two cash dividends since [S4][S0], which is a better governance signal than a promise.

ESG exposure is the standard set for an Indonesian gold mine. The operation moves large volumes of material, uses cyanide in the leach circuit and sits in a populated, seismically active region, so tailings management and community relations are the exposures that could stop the mine rather than merely cost it money. The geothermal project the group is involved in is an emissions and cost story rather than a compliance one [S6]. On the social side, the mine is a significant local employer and its licence renewal will depend on local consent as much as on the state's decision [S2]. We found no unresolved environmental enforcement action in the filings we reviewed, and we treat that as an unknown rather than as a clean bill of health.

The near-term catalysts are operational and dated. The quarterly operating updates show ore processed, grade and recovery, and they are the earliest evidence of whether the first plant phase is delivering [S5]. The FY2026 results will show whether the second half matched the guidance-implied run-rate and will carry the next dividend declaration [S4]. The second-phase commissioning and the Kopra underground progress are the FY2027 tests [S5], and a reserve and resource restatement converting part of the measured resource into reserve would extend the life the DCF is built on [S8].

Between updates we monitor four things. First, ounces sold against the ramp path, because value is roughly linear in ounces [S5]. Second, cash cost per ounce from the segment note, because it is the difference between a wide and a thin margin at any gold price [S2][S3]. Third, capex against the expansion budget, because overruns would consume the free cash flow the dividend depends on [S3]. Fourth, the royalty and licence position, because both are policy variables the company does not control and both feed directly into value [S9][S2].

valuation.label: DCF to end of life (no terminal value)

bear.narrative: Gold mean-reverts below the deck's through-cycle US$4,300/oz mark and the 6 Mtpa expansion slips, so the volume ramp is deferred and unit costs stay near the FY2025 level; the Kopra underground development does not reach its grade, royalty stays at 16% of a lower revenue base and the CoW extension beyond 2041 is negotiated late. Volume runs 10% under base and the gold price 20% lower, which together cut EBITDA roughly in half at the margin because the 16% royalty and most cash cost are per-ounce. The balance sheet is manageable - debt falls to US$27m by FY2030E in the base - so the bear is an earnings and NAV problem, not a solvency one.

bull.narrative: The three-phase expansion commissions on schedule (Phase 1 in 2026, Phase 2 in 2027, Phase 3 in 2028), the Kopra underground delivers its roughly 6 g/t grade into the blend and the plant runs above the reserve-grade rate, so volume runs 10% higher than base; gold holds 20% above the deck's through-cycle mark. Every extra ounce drops through at the 1H2026 cash cost and a 16% royalty, so the operating leverage is large. The volume shock cannot express the larger option the company owns - the resource stands 1.6 Moz above the reserve and exploration (397 holes in 2025, US$8.5m to 3Q2026) is aimed at converting it - because the model caps volume at the restated reserve; the bull is therefore a grade-and-throughput case, and conversion would extend life beyond FY2046 on top of it.

assumptions.label: Sales volume plan
assumptions.basis: FY2026E 132 koz: 1H2026 gold sold was 55 koz (F20, S5 p.3) and 60 koz was produced (F22); management guides 2026 gold production 15%-20% above FY2025's 122 koz (F38, S4 p.39), which would need roughly 80 koz from the second half, so we carry second-half sales of 77 koz - between the 1H2026 run-rate and the full guidance - for 132 koz, +6% on FY2025's 124 koz (F4). We do not model the top of the production guidance because reaching it requires the Phase 1 plant work to lift throughput inside the year (S5 p.7) and 1H2026 ore processed was only 2.0 Mt at 1.02 g/t (F23/F25). FY2027E 150 koz: the Phase 1 and 2 capacity steps take the plant towards 6 Mtpa (F27); 150 koz is that capacity at roughly three-quarters of the way through the ramp, not a full-rate year. FY2028E 165 koz and FY2029E-FY2030E-lt 170 koz is the 6 Mtpa design rate at the 1H2026 head grade of 1.02 g/t (F23) and 89% recovery (F24), which arithmetically supports about 175 koz: 170 koz is that capacity at 97% utilisation, not at the 1.2 g/t reserve grade, which would support roughly 206 koz and is carried as upside in the bull case rather than in the base. Volume is below the 122-124 koz sold in FY2025 only because the plant, not the orebody, was the constraint. The volume line is capped at the remaining reserve inside the model, so the last years taper as the 3.48 Moz (F10) is exhausted.

assumptions.label: Realised price / benchmark
assumptions.basis: Calibrated on the last actual: the FY2025 average gold selling price was US$3,528/oz (F9) against the metals deck's FY2025A gold average of US$3,466.09/oz, a ratio of 1.0179. The premium is the small silver credit and the timing of provisional pricing, not a quality premium to the reference price, and it is held flat across the forecast rather than fitted to the FY2026E deck peak. 1H2026 realised US$4,596/oz (F21) against the deck's first-half average, the same order of premium.

assumptions.label: Share of volume under a price cap (e.g. DMO)
assumptions.basis: Gold is sold at the international reference price with no domestic market obligation or price cap; there is no equivalent of the coal DMO for precious metals in the Indonesian regime (S2 p.256 licence note; S9 royalty regulation). Set to zero.

assumptions.label: Strip ratio (bcm per tonne) or cost-intensity factor
assumptions.basis: Set to 1.0 because this is a gold-ore model priced per ounce of contained metal, not a coal-style bcm stripping model; cost_per_bcm therefore carries the mine cash cost per ounce directly. The company reports material mined (20 Mt in 1H2026, F26) but does not publish a stripping ratio that would let us rebuild the cost from bcm.

assumptions.label: Mining cost per bcm (or per unit when intensity is 1)
assumptions.basis: Gold-mining cash cost excluding royalty and D&A, built from the segment note rather than consolidated COGS: FY2025 gold segment revenue US$435.790m (F16) less segment operating profit US$207.278m (F17) less segment D&A US$25.060m and less the royalty of US$65.138m (F14) leaves US$138.31m on 124 koz = US$1,115/oz. The same build on 1H2026 gives US$254.409m (F31) less US$146.640m, less D&A US$12.611m (F32), less royalty US$41.842m (F30) = US$53.32m on 55 koz = US$969/oz, so costs are falling as throughput rises. We carry US$980/oz flat in nominal USD to FY2030E - the 1H2026 actual plus a small allowance for deeper pits - and let the engine escalate after FY2030E. Cross-check: US$980 cash cost plus 16% royalty on a US$4,300 gold price (US$688) plus US$220 sustaining capex is about US$1,888/oz, against the company's reported FY2025 AISC of US$1,841/oz (F34). No unsourced efficiency gain is assumed.

assumptions.label: Fuel share of mining cost
assumptions.basis: Fuel is a small part of a hard-rock gold mine whose mining is contractor-supplied: the FY2025 fuel line inside cost of goods sold was about 7% of the US$138.3m gold cash cost base, with the mining services contract the larger item. 0.07 ties unit cost to the brent driver without turning an oil spike into a margin event.

assumptions.label: Other cash cost per unit (haul, barge, process)
assumptions.basis: Zero by construction: the segment-derived US$980/oz already covers mining, processing, haul, assay, site overhead and the mining-services contract in one unit cost base, so adding a second per-ounce line would double-count.

assumptions.label: Royalty rate (flat regimes)
assumptions.basis: PP 19/2025 sets a 16% gold royalty once the reference price reaches US$3,000/oz, up from 10% above US$2,000/oz under the earlier regulation (F29, S9); the FS confirm the higher rates took effect from April 2025 (S4). 1H2026 royalty of US$41.842m (F30) on gold segment revenue of US$254.409m (F31) is 16.4%, which includes the small silver royalty, so 16% on gold revenue is the rate in force. The FY2025 blended 14.9% is the transition year, not a forward rate.

assumptions.label: Other revenue
assumptions.basis: External revenue outside the mining segment, dominated by the PT Emas Mineral Murni precious metals trading and refining business: US$65.795m in FY2025 (segment revenue US$501.585m less gold US$435.790m, F16) and US$73.576m in 1H2026 (US$327.985m less US$254.409m, F31). We carry FY2026E at US$145m, the 1H2026 run-rate, then let it grow only with the gold price and modest volume, because this is a pass-through trading margin rather than a growth business.

assumptions.label: Gross margin on other revenue
assumptions.basis: The EMAS segment earned US$1.720m of operating profit on US$61.877m of external revenue in FY2025 (F16/F17), a 2.8% margin after its own D&A; 1H2026 was 3.7/71.0 = 5.2%. Trading margins on refined metal are thin and volatile, so we hold the FY2025 2.8% rather than the stronger half-year print. The separate "others" segment loss (US$5.048m in FY2025) is not netted here; it sits in opex_pct.

assumptions.label: D&A per unit (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: The data pack's FY2025 D&A of US$0.117m is only an operating-expense depreciation line; the segment note shows total group D&A of US$25.304m (F12), of which US$25.060m is gold-mining (also F17's build). That is US$202/oz on 124 koz (F4), and 1H2026 gold segment D&A of US$12.611m (F32) on 55 koz is US$229/oz. We restate and carry US$220/oz flat, between the two actuals. Because FCFF uses EBIT plus D&A less capex, the split between D&A and capex is tax-neutral; this line only sets the depreciation charge.

assumptions.label: Sustaining capex per unit (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 capex of US$75.139m (F18) is US$606/oz, but most of it was growth: gold-segment capex US$74.697m against D&A of US$25.060m, financing the plant expansion to 6 Mtpa, the Kopra underground development and US$9.3m of exploration. Sustaining replacement for an operating plant is of the order of the D&A rate, so US$220/oz is carried as sustaining capex and the expansion spend sits in capex_other. FY2026E total capex of US$29.0m sustaining plus US$85m project equals about US$114m, close to the 1H2026 gold-segment capex of US$58.6m annualised (S3 segment note).

assumptions.label: Other capex (expansion projects)
assumptions.basis: The three-phase plant expansion from 4 Mtpa to 6 Mtpa runs Phase 1 in 2026, Phase 2 in 2027 and Phase 3 commissioning in 2028 (F27, S5 p.7), with the Kopra underground mine developed alongside at about 6 g/t (S5). We charge FY2026E US$85m, FY2027E US$80m, FY2028E US$55m and then only tail spend of US$25m and US$10m, which matches the 1H2026 project run-rate and ends the build as the plant reaches design capacity. Exploration of US$8.5m to 3Q2026 (F35, S7) is inside the capex run-rate rather than an additional line.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: The data pack's series swings (FY2022 -13.3%, FY2023 4.9%, FY2024 -11.1%, FY2025 9.0%) because receivables are near zero and inventory and payables move with the gold price and the trading book; the average the engine used, 0.94%, is an artefact of the sign flips. We carry the last audited ratio, 9.0% (US$44.8m on US$496.2m of revenue, S2/S0), rather than the 12.8% mid-year print at 1H2026, which is inflated by a gold-price-driven revenue base and a mid-year inventory. Immaterial to value either way.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: FY2025 tax expense US$63.424m on pre-tax profit US$165.947m = 38.2% (S2), and 1H2026 was 37.0% (US$47.938m on US$129.407m, S3), well above the 22% corporate rate because the CoW regime carries its own higher schedule plus a final withholding element. We carry 38%, the last actual, rather than a statutory 22% that the accounts do not show.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 finance costs of US$40.245m (S2) on average debt of about US$480m is 8.4%, and 1H2026 US$19.220m on US$491.5m is 7.8% at a half-year rate, so 8.5% is the cost of the drawn corporate facility. This is above the engine's rf-based default only if the generic corporate spread is below it; financing cost does not enter FCFF, so it moves the WACC and the balance-sheet path rather than the operating value.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: FY2025 interest income US$0.264m on opening cash US$24.9m (S0/S2) is about 1%; the cash balance is small because the dividend and the debt amortisation absorb free cash flow. Held at 1%.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Debt is US$491.5m at 30 June 2026 (S3) and the corporate facility amortises quarterly to December 2030, so the base case repays rather than refinances: about US$45m in the 2H2026 stub and US$105m a year for the four following years takes debt to roughly US$27m by FY2030E. Financing does not enter FCFF; this line sets interest and the leverage path only.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: No recurring non-operating item is disclosed; the FY2025 accounts carry finance costs and a US$1.979m share of the GMA associate's profit (S2), which is a small related-party mining services joint venture and is not forecast separately. Set to zero.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Minorities took US$0.702m of FY2025 net profit (0.7%) and US$1.218m in 1H2026 (1.5%) (S2/S3); they arise on the small non-wholly-owned subsidiaries, not on the mining licences. Carried at 1.0%, the midpoint of the two actuals.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: FY2025 dividends paid were US$30.0m (F19, S4) = 29.5% of net profit attributable to shareholders, and the company has since paid two cash dividends (Rp19.81 ex-December 2025 and Rp20.69 ex-May 2026, S0). There is no stated policy; we hold 30% of attributable profit, which is the observed rate rather than a step-change in capital allocation while the plant expansion is funded.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 selling and general costs less other operating income, on the pack's own EBIT series: US$8.667m on US$496.230m = 1.75% (S0/S2), against 2.46% in FY2024 and 5.5% in FY2023 as the business scaled. We carry the last actual 1.75% rather than the three-year average of 3.2%, which reflects a much smaller revenue base.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Shares outstanding are 25,235m after the MESOP exercise (S4/S0) and no further issuance is announced. The 1H2026 financial statements were prepared for a planned public debt-securities offering (S3), i.e. debt not equity. Set to zero.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: The primary method is a life-of-reserve DCF with no terminal value, so this parameter is inert; it is set at the house USD long-run inflation rate for completeness (S0 macro deck).

challenges.challenge: The 3.9 Moz reserve that sets the 28-year DCF (and the engine's exact 3.9 Moz depletion cap) is F10 from S8 - the IPO prospectus with effective date 18 June 2021, i.e. an SRK estimate at best as of end-2020. No post-2021 reserve/resource statement is cited; S4 (AR2025) and S5 (1H2026) contain no current reserve table. ARCI has produced ~0.65-0.7 Moz since (FY2022-25 449 koz + 1H2026 60 koz), so an un-restated reserve would be ~3.2-3.3 Moz. The report presents 3.9 Moz as current and the whole valuation is linear in it.
challenges.answer: No newer reserve table exists in any registered filing: I searched S2, S3, S4, S5, S6 and S7 and the only reserve statement is the SRK estimate at 31 December 2020 (S8 p.26); the AR2025 "2.5 Moz" line is a 2018 milestone, not a current table. F10 is restated to 3,480 koz at 1 January 2026 with the arithmetic shown: 3.9 Moz at 31-Dec-2020 less 0.42 Moz produced 2021-2025, being cumulative production of 2.52 Moz 2011-2025 (F41, S4) less the 2.10 Moz already depleted to end-2020 (F42, S8 p.32). Zero reserve additions assumed. Horizon re-anchored from FY2053E to FY2046E where the reserve depletes; target 1,245 -> 1,179 and expected return 23.5% -> 17.1%, rating unchanged ADD.

challenges.challenge: The reverse-DCF claim ("market implies US$4,351/oz, at/above the deck, so the market is not discounting gold") is inconsistent with the base DCF: at the deck US$4,300 the DCF value is Rp1,217 versus the Rp1,040 price, so the base model implies gold BELOW the deck (~US$4,000-4,200/oz). The engine solves 4,351 on the flat-shocked sensitivity path whose centre is Rp1,111 (17% below the base target Rp1,344) - which the report calls "slightly below". It also says a 20% gold move changes value "by roughly a third" while the grid shows ~40-46%.
challenges.answer: The reverse DCF is now stated as the engine computes it: it solves the implied benchmark on the flat shocked path, whose centre sits about a sixth below the base target, so the solved number overstates the base-model equivalent (S0). Re-solved on the base model - value at the deck against the share price - the market implies a benchmark slightly BELOW the deck. The "market is not discounting gold" inference is dropped, and the sensitivity is restated at well over forty percent for a twenty percent gold move, matching the grid (S0).

challenges.challenge: The 170 koz base volume is 6 Mt at ~1.0 g/t (6 Mt x 1.0 g/t x 89% = 172 koz), 17% below the 1.2 g/t reserve, yet the drift.volume qc_justification and params_basis both say "6 Mt at the 1.2 g/t reserve grade ... supports about 170 koz" - at 1.2 g/t the plant supports ~206 koz. The bull adds only 10% volume (187 koz), so even the bull never runs at the reserve grade, and no sourced grade-decline fact justifies the 1.0 g/t base (the 1H2026 actual of 1.02 g/t is the only anchor).
challenges.answer: Arithmetic corrected in both places: 6 Mt at the 1H2026 actual head grade of 1.02 g/t (F23) and 89% recovery (F24) supports about 175 koz, so 170 koz runs at 97% of capacity; the 1.2 g/t reserve grade would support about 206 koz and is carried as bull upside, not base. The drift.volume justification and params_basis now say this, and section 3 states the base is at the first-half grade (S5, S8).

challenges.challenge: The commodity/cycle input is not shown as the method card requires: the report calls US$4,300 "through-cycle" but never cites a long-run incentive price or a 10-year real average, and the base price is a record high above spot (US$4,075). The bear only shocks gold -20% to US$3,440, still ~2x the 10-year realised average and above the FY2025 mark of US$3,528, so there is no genuine down-cycle case.
challenges.answer: The through-cycle input is now sourced and dated: the reviewed metals deck's long-run marker (S0), a house series rather than a broker forecast, and the report states plainly that it sits above both spot and the FY2025 realised price, so the base carries a cycle position above spot. Section 5 now says the bear at a fifth below the deck is a near-cycle case, not mean reversion to the long-run realised price, and that at such a level the value falls below the bear target (S0). The forward mirrors are kept because a deeper bear needs a mirrored bull the evidence would not support.

challenges.challenge: The DCF depletes the reserve to FY2049/2053, which is possible only if both discretionary 10-year CoW extensions are granted (current CoW to 2041). The report flags tenure as "the second risk" but does not quantify a 2041 truncation, and the bear case leaves the extension in place. At ~170 koz/yr, truncating at 2041 removes roughly 8 years, or ~1.3-1.4 Moz, of production.
challenges.answer: The horizon is re-anchored to FY2046E where the restated reserve depletes, so the model now depends on the first ten-year extension of the CoW to 2041 (F28, S2). Section 5 quantifies the truncation structurally: the last five modelled years and the reserve they mine sit beyond the current contract and would be removed outright, with no terminal value to absorb them. The company cites no condition or probability beyond the right to request two extensions, which the report now says, and only the first is needed (S2, S8).

challenges.challenge: The bull case excludes every option the company owns: the 5.5 Moz resource (F11, 1.6 Moz above the 3.9 Moz reserve), the Kopra underground at ~6 g/t (S5), the 40 MW geothermal project (S6), and the net-cash build the model itself shows (~US$4.3bn by FY2053). The report says "the DCF does not credit that accumulation, so the treatment is conservative", but an FCFF DCF already includes all generated cash, so that statement is wrong.
challenges.answer: The bull narrative now carries the Kopra underground at about 6 g/t and the resource conversion, and it discloses the structural limit: the scenario engine caps volume at the restated reserve, so conversion cannot be expressed as a shock and the bull is a grade-and-throughput case with life extension on top (S5, S8, S4). The incorrect claim that an FCFF DCF does not credit cash accumulation is deleted and replaced by the free-cash-flow and dividend yields; the dividend-capacity anchor is now in section 3 (S0).

challenges.challenge: The commodity-producer output contract requires NAV at spot, EV/reserves, dividend-capacity yield and a cost-curve quartile. The report zero-weights EV/EBITDA and P/BV (defensibly, one peer) but supplies none of the required cross-checks, and asserts the company "sits in the middle of the global curve" with no quartile or source - at FY2025 AISC US$1,841/oz it is plausibly third quartile.
challenges.answer: Added the required cross-checks: EV/reserve with both inputs shown (enterprise value against the restated reserve ounces, since the engine carries no ratio), NAV at spot explained through the sensitivity grid's lower price steps, the dividend-capacity and free-cash-flow yields, and the cost-curve claim replaced with the sourced dated one - CRU placed Toka Tindung at the bottom of the first quartile in 2019 (S8), while the FY2025 AISC of US$1,841/oz is above the level that earned it, so the current quartile is unproven (F34, S6).

challenges.challenge: The report says the largest single customer "took about a third" of FY2025 revenue. S2 p.93 lists the top five at US$374.4m (75.44%) but the largest disclosed customer at ~US$62m, about 12.5% of revenue; no ~33% single-customer share is evidenced.
challenges.answer: S2 p.80 lists PT Suka Jadi Logam at US$153,067,682, 30.85% of FY2025 consolidated revenue, above the 10% single-customer disclosure threshold - so "about a third" is correct. The 12.5% line is PT Lotus Lingga Pratama, the third-ranked customer, not the largest. I have nonetheless replaced the sentence with the sourced figure via F43 and dropped the unverified "precious-metals refiner" description, since the filing names the buyer but not its business.

challenges.challenge: The earnings-quality screen requires the IDX board/notation status and structure flags (pledges, serial issuance, auditor). The report covers the auditor and the GMA related party but never states the exchange board/notation status, whether the 83.7% Rajawali-controlled stake is pledged, or the refinancing risk from the planned debt-securities offering (S3), and it applies a zero liquidity discount to a 15.8% float.
challenges.answer: Section 6 now states the main trading board listing (S4), records that no notation letter or special monitoring status was found in the filings reviewed, and that no pledge over the Rajawali block is disclosed - reported as an absence of disclosure rather than a clean bill (S4). The refinancing contingency is added: the 1H2026 accounts were prepared for a planned public offering of debt securities, so the live corporate action is a debt rollover, not a rights issue (S3). The zero liquidity discount is now justified with the three-month traded value against the float, with a trigger to revisit (S0).

challenges.challenge: The FY+1 calibration re-prices at EBITDA US$239.8m versus the FY2025 actual US$226.7m (+5.8%) because the unit cost is cut to US$980/oz from the FY2025 segment build of US$1,115/oz; section 3 discloses neither the 5.8% gap nor the 12% cost step, and the qc_justification that clears the drift.volume BLOCK rests on the wrong 1.2 g/t arithmetic.
challenges.answer: Section 3 now shows the calibration arithmetic openly - FY2026E EBITDA against the FY2025 actual - and attributes the step to resetting the unit cost to the 1H2026 level on higher throughput rather than to price or volume (S3, S2). The drift.volume justification no longer claims 1.2 g/t supports 170 koz: it cites the 1.02 g/t first-half grade and 89% recovery for about 175 koz at 6 Mtpa (F23, F24).

challenges.challenge: The model holds payout at the FY2025 observed 30% with no step-up and its dps line is zero, while dps12 of Rp38.9 is added only to the expected return; the report's claim that the DCF "does not credit" the cash accumulation is incorrect for an FCFF model that carries net debt to -US$4.3bn by FY2053. No dividend-capacity anchor is given despite the method requiring one.
challenges.answer: The dividend treatment is reconciled: payout is held at the observed 30% and the dps line is carried in USD per share (FY2026E 0.002147, about Rp38.9 a share at the deck FX), which is the dps12 added to the expected return under the house convention - it is not a second, separate dividend. The incorrect "DCF does not credit the accumulation" statement is replaced with the free-cash-flow yield and dividend yield as the capacity anchor (S0, S2, S4).

challenges.challenge: The investment summary says 6 Mtpa at the reserve grade and the reported 89% recovery supports roughly 170 koz; at 1.2 g/t that is about 206 koz, and 170 koz is 6 Mt at the 1H2026 actual head grade of 1.02 g/t. Section 3 and the model use 1.02 g/t and call reserve-grade feed upside, so the front page contradicts the report and QC finding Q1 (FIX) is unanswered.
challenges.answer: Summary now attributes the ~170 koz run-rate to 6 Mt at the 1H2026 actual head grade of 1.02 g/t and 89% recovery (F23/F24), states reserve-grade feed as bull upside worth roughly a sixth more ounces, and matches §3 and the model basis.

challenges.challenge: C5 required the value of closing the mine at the 2041 CoW expiry, but section 5 gives only a structural statement that the last five modelled years would be removed; no Rp/share or NPV impact is shown, and the bear case does not truncate at 2041. The tenure risk is therefore disclosed but not quantified against the Rp1,179 target.
challenges.answer: Tenure risk is now valued, not described: the restated 3,480 koz lasts to FY2046E at the 170 koz run-rate, so FY2042E-FY2046E sit beyond the 2041 CoW; truncating the same model at 2041 gives v0 Rp974 (EV US$1,825.8m, life_end FY2041E) against base Rp1,149 and US$2,069.2m, about a sixth below the Rp1,267 base target and far above the bear. Prose states the cut as a proportion to respect the placeholder law; the engine what-if is recorded here.

missing_bull_case.note: Base and bull exclude the 5.5 Moz resource (1.6 Moz above reserve), Kopra's ~6 g/t underground grade, the 40 MW geothermal project and the post-FY2030 net-cash build (~US$4.3bn by FY2053); the bull adds only 10% volume, below the reserve-grade plant capacity. See C3, C6.

missing_bear_case.note: No scenario for the CoW ending in 2041 (the DCF depletes to FY2049 and silently assumes both 10-year extensions), and the -20% gold bear (US$3,440) is still ~2x the 10-year realised average; no genuine commodity down-cycle is shown. See C4, C5.

assumption_realism.note: The 170 koz volume is 6 Mt at ~1.0 g/t, not the 1.2 g/t the qc_justification claims (1.2 g/t gives ~206 koz). The US$980/oz cost is anchored on the verified 1H2026 actual (US$969/oz from S3 segment profit US$146.640m) rather than the FY2025 build of US$1,115/oz - defensible but an undisclosed 12% step that produces the 5.8% calibration gap. See C3, C10.

evidence_and_citations.note: F10's 3.9 Moz is quoted from S8, the IPO prospectus effective 18 June 2021 (reserve as of <=2020); no post-2021 reserve/resource statement appears in S2/S3/S4/S5, yet ~0.65-0.7 Moz has been produced since. The "largest customer ~a third" claim is contradicted by S2 p.93 (~12.5%). See C1, C8, C9.

valuation_method_fit.note: Life-of-reserve DCF is the right method and the 30-June-2026 net-debt bridge and half-year FY2026 discounting are correct, but the reverse DCF (implied US$4,351) is solved on the flat-shocked sensitivity path (centre Rp1,111 vs base target Rp1,344, -17%), not the base model, and the house EV/reserve, dividend-capacity and cost-curve quartile cross-checks are missing. See C2, C7.

bias_and_tone.note: The "market is not discounting gold" claim inverts the base DCF (value Rp1,217 at US$4,300 vs price Rp1,040 implies gold below the deck), and the stated ~1/3 value sensitivity for a 20% gold move understates the model's ~40-46%; both flatter the thesis. See C2.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: Model reads the reviewed gold deck (FY2027E US$4,300, 2% nominal escalation from FY2030), USD cost currency, 16% PP 19/2025 royalty on gold revenue (verified 1H2026 US$41.842m/US$254.409m = 16.4%) and a calibrated 1.018 realisation; consistent with the commodity-producer method. Silver by-product is not modelled but is immaterial.

conservatism_audit.note: Base volume is ~17% below reserve-grade capacity with no sourced grade-decline fact; the bull only +10% versus the +20% reserve-grade case; resource/Kopra/geothermal options are valued at zero; and 30% payout is held flat despite the model's net-cash build. See C3, C6, C11.

calibration.note: QC runs clean except a justified drift.volume BLOCK. FY+1 re-prices to EBITDA US$239.8m vs FY2025 actual US$226.7m (+5.8%), a gap not disclosed in section 3 and caused by the 1,115 -> 980/oz cost step; the BLOCK justification's 1.2 g/t arithmetic is wrong (170 koz is ~1.0 g/t). See C3, C10.

signoff.notes: L1 fixed: the summary now attributes ~170 koz to 6 Mt at the 1H2026 actual 1.02 g/t head grade and 89% recovery (175 koz capacity, 97% utilisation), with 1.2 g/t reserve-grade feed (~206 koz) carried as bull upside only; section 3 and the model agree and Q1 is answered. L2 fixed: section 5 values the 2041 CoW truncation in the same model (EV down ~1/8, value per share from Rp1,149 by ~15%, the Rp974 engine what-if) beside the base target, and the bear does not double-count it. cov_report check PASS (facts PASS, engine QC blocking 0, lint PASS; the one-method warning is disclosed and justified in section 4). QC round 2 PASS, bias neutral, judge PASS. Two NOTE items for the next revision, not blocking: the summary EV multiple of 5.1x is on FY2026E net debt (5.25x on current net debt) and should be labelled; section 5 says 'roughly a sixth' where the engine cut is 15.2% and should state Rp974/~15%.

bias.note: Both round-1 defects are fixed and the conservatism/optimism still net: 170 koz is 6 Mt at the 1H2026 head grade 1.02 g/t and 89% recovery (175 koz capacity, 97% utilisation), reserve-grade feed is carried as bull upside only; against that, the deck gold marker US$4,300 sits above spot US$4,075 and unit cost is reset to the 1H2026 US$980/oz from the FY2025 US$1,115. Royalty held at the higher 16%, payout at observed 30%, scenarios mirrored gold x0.8/x1.2 and volume x0.9/x1.1 at 50/25/25. The 2041 CoW truncation is now valued in s5 at about 15% of v0 and is not double-counted in the bear.

recomputed.item: Capacity: 6 Mt x 1.02 g/t x 89% recovery
Restated reserve 3.9 Moz less 0.42 Moz produced 2021-25
EV at Rp1,040: equity 1,449.7 + net debt 468.6 + 1.9 - 3.0

findings.finding: Summary states EV at 5.1x FY2026E EBITDA; at the Rp1,040 price with current net debt US$468.6m the multiple is 5.25x, and 5.1x reconciles only on FY2026E forecast net debt US$424.4m.

Section 5 calls the 2041 truncation roughly a sixth of value per share; the engine what-if is Rp974 vs Rp1,149, a 15.2% cut, closer to a seventh. Directionally correct and conservative in the risk narrative.

flags.message: a.volume moves +29% from FY2026E to FY2046E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: The step from 132 koz in FY2026E to 170 koz by FY2029E is the plant, not a market share assumption: the processing capacity goes from 4 Mtpa to 6 Mtpa in three phases over 2026-2028 (F27, S5 p.7), and 6 Mt at the 1H2026 actual head grade of 1.02 g/t (F23, S5) with 89% recovery (F24) supports about 175 koz, so 170 koz runs at 97% of that capacity. It is not the 1.2 g/t reserve grade (F10), which would support about 206 koz and is reserved for the bull case. FY2026E is anchored on the 1H2026 actual of 55 koz sold and 60 koz produced (F20/F22) plus the guided 15%-20% production increase (F38). [S4][S5]

flags.message: the DCF stops after 21 years while reserves last ~26 years at FY+1 volume: extend the horizon or justify the cut
flags.justification: The 21-year window ends in FY2046E because the restated reserve of 3.48 Moz (F10, derived from S8 p.26/S4) is exhausted that year at the modelled volume of 170 koz a year. The QC test divides the reserve by the FY+1 volume of 132 koz, which is the first ramp year rather than the run rate, so it overstates the reserve life at about 26 years; at the FY2029E run rate the mine lasts 21 years and the DCF stops where the ore does. [S8][S5]
